title: Quantization-Aware Training for Ultra-Low-Bit Reasoning LLMs
one_liner: A two-stage training pipeline that shrinks language models to 2-bit weights while keeping their reasoning ability intact by first stabilizing the network with mixed data, then fixing reasoning loss with a teacher.
lead: Language models are huge and expensive to run. Quantization (shrinking each number from 32 bits to 2 bits) makes them tiny, but it usually breaks their ability to reason through multi-step problems. This paper shows that the problem comes from how knowledge gets baked in during training, and fixes it with a two-step approach: first, stabilize the tiny weights using many kinds of data; second, use a trained teacher to fix the reasoning damage.

paras: Language models (trained neural networks that predict the next word) are so big they cost huge money to run. Quantization shrinks each stored number from 32 binary digits down to 2 digits, cutting memory and speed 16-fold. But when you shrink a network built to reason, something breaks: the model loses the ability to follow multi-step logic, solve math problems, or trace through complex ideas.

A beginner tries to just quantize after training is done (shrink the weights and hope). This fails because reasoning capability lives in subtle relationships between weights. Those relationships are fragile. Squeezing numbers into 2-bit bins destroys the delicate balance. The network can still spit out grammatical text, but it cannot think through problems anymore.

callout.html: Shrinking a reasoning model's numbers breaks the internal logic it learned.

steps.text: Quantize using examples from many domains (code, math, language) to learn which numbers matter most.
Fine-tune the 2-bit model using a full-size teacher that scores reasoning steps, steering it back toward correct logic.
Test on math and logic problems to verify the tiny model still solves them.
Show that this two-stage approach beats simpler methods by a huge margin.
Run the 2-bit model on cheap hardware while keeping reasoning intact.

paras: The paper changes how the quantization rule is learned and applied. Instead of a single fixed squashing rule, it uses calibration data from many domains to discover which weights matter most, then fine-tunes the result using a teacher model. The network learns a smarter way to shrink.

hidden.name: Reasoning survival rate
paras: This measures a concrete thing: what fraction of multi-step problems does the tiny model still solve correctly after shrinking? A question like 'If Alice has 5 apples and Bob has 3 times as many, how many do they have together?' requires tracking numbers, applying operations, and combining them. This score is: shrunken model accuracy divided by original model accuracy, across reasoning-heavy test sets.

The paper estimates this by running the quantized model on standard benchmarks and comparing accuracy to the full-size baseline. Mixed-domain calibration preserves this score much better because it prevents the network from overspecializing to just one task and losing its general reasoning muscle.

heat.caption: Darker means reasoning survives shrinking better; lighter tasks suffer more.

reads.html: How much of the model's problem-solving brain stays intact when you shrink its numbers?
Accuracy on reasoning benchmarks (GSM8K math, logic puzzles) as a fraction of original full-precision accuracy.

paras: A naive quantization rule squashes all weights based on size alone: big weights get big 2-bit codes, small weights get tiny codes. But reasoning lives in the relationships between weights, not just their sizes. A global rule cannot capture that. Making it worse, if you train the quantization rule on just one type of data (say, only math problems), the network learns to compress for math but forgets how to handle language or code.

The fix: two stages, both needed. First, learn the quantization rule using examples from many domains (math, code, language, instructions). The network discovers which weights matter across all types of knowledge, not just one. This universal rule preserves the broad reasoning structure. Second, take the quantized model and fine-tune it using a teacher—a full-size model that sees each reasoning task and scores whether the 2-bit model did it correctly. The fine-tuning loss punishes mistakes the teacher flagged, rewarding paths the teacher approved. This targeted steering repairs the damage quantization caused to reasoning pathways. Unlike single-task methods, mixing domains keeps reasoning knowledge spread across all tasks instead of compressed into just one.

stages.s: Full-size trained model with reasoning ability
Gather calibration examples: math, code, language, instructions
Learn universal 2-bit quantization rule from mixed data
Assign 2-bit codes using the learned rule
Teacher model rates reasoning correctness on each step

math.words: Total loss equals the base training loss (how accurate the model is on tasks) plus a quantization penalty that keeps the 2-bit weights close to the original weights, with the penalty strength set by how important each weight is across all domains, plus a teacher-guided reward term that steers reasoning toward solutions the teacher approved.
math.equation: L = L_base + lambda_q * sum_i c_i * (w_i_quant - w_i_orig)^2 + lambda_r * L_teacher
symbols: base task loss (accuracy on reasoning benchmarks)
how much to penalize weight drift
calibration importance score for weight i (learned from mixed domains)
original full-precision value of weight i
how much to trust the teacher
penalty for reasoning steps the teacher marked as wrong

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Weight w1 is originally 3.7. Quantization assigns it 2.0. Calibration says this weight matters a lot across domains: c_1 = 0.8.
Teacher says one reasoning step using w1 went wrong. L_teacher contribution: 0.5.
L_base is 0.8 (model gets 80% of task accuracy). Lambda_q is 0.1, lambda_r is 0.2.
If we adjust w1 from 2.0 to 2.5, drift becomes (2.5 - 3.7)^2 = 1.44, weighted = 1.15. New total loss = 0.8 + 0.115 + 0.1 = 1.015. Training learns to make that adjustment.

math.note: The calibration importance scores (learned from mixed domains) tell the network which weights must stay precise. The teacher loss steers specific reasoning steps in the right direction.

charts.title: Post-training quantization (naive baseline)
charts.note: Shrinking the numbers breaks reasoning. Big drop because no guidance during compression.

charts.title: This paper: two-stage QAT
charts.note: Mixed-domain calibration and teacher guidance preserve reasoning. Only small drop from original.

items.html: If the mixed-domain calibration data does not include examples from the reasoning task you care about, the quantization rule will not adapt well. A model calibrated on code and language but never math problems will struggle on math.
If the teacher model itself makes mistakes on reasoning, it will teach the 2-bit model to copy those mistakes. The teacher must be reliable.
If you fine-tune the 2-bit model too aggressively with the teacher, it may memorize the training reasoning steps and fail on new, unseen problems.

Use diverse calibration data, a high-quality teacher, and careful regularization to prevent over-fitting. Balance the two-stage process: enough calibration to preserve structure, enough teacher guidance to fix reasoning, but not so much that it memorizes.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small reasoning model (about 100 million numbers to adjust during training), train it on a subset of math word problems. Split the test set in half. On the first half, quantize it naively (post-training quantization) and measure reasoning accuracy. On the second half, run the two-stage pipeline: calibrate with mixed examples (math, code, plain text) and then fine-tune with a full-size teacher. Show the accuracy gap. It should be dramatic: naive drops 40-50%, two-stage drops only 5-10%.
demo.closing: The two-stage pipeline nearly restores all reasoning ability even in a 2-bit model, while naive quantization destroys it. That difference is real and measurable.
